name: Arabic tahwidah (تهويدة, cradle song)
lineage: Pan-Arab lullaby tradition (the term tahwidah cognate with the Arabic verb hawwada, 'to lull/soothe'), regional variants across Levantine, Maghrebi, Egyptian, Yemeni, and Gulf-Arabian traditions. Sung by mothers-and-grandmothers in informal domestic-context with no instrumental accompaniment, the tahwidah employs free-rhythm slow-tempo melismatic-ornamentation drawing on classical-maqam modal-vocabulary (Bayati, Rast, and Hijaz being the most common for lullabies). Lyrics typically address the child directly (often with regional-dialectal diminutives) and reference religious-protection invocations, mother's-and-grandmother's wishes-for-the-child, and pastoral imagery. The tradition has been disproportionately preserved by ethnomusicological field-recordings since the 1960s due to its private-domestic context being underrepresented in commercial-recording.
